subject: Anthropology
title: Informal Economy
description: A micro-lesson that makes Informal Economy usable.

hook.text: Street vendors, day laborers, and home businesses. The informal economy is invisible to governments but feeds billions.

buildup.text: The informal economy includes all economic activity outside state regulation — untaxed, unregistered, and undocumented.

discovery.text: Keith Hart coined the term studying workers in Ghana who survived outside formal employment through creative hustle.

twist.text: The informal sector isn't a failure of development. It's how most of the world actually works and survives.

climax.text: Ignoring informal economies means ignoring how billions live. Formal models miss the majority of global economic life.

punchline.text: The real economy often works off the books.

quiz.question: What is the informal economy?
options: Economic activity outside state regulation and formal employment
A small part of any economy

details.summary: The informal economy encompasses all economic activity outside state regulation and taxation — street vending, domestic work, day labor, and underground markets. Rather than marginal.
details.whyItMatters: The informal economy challenges the assumption that formal market employment is normal and informal work is deviant. In much of the world, informal economic activity is the primary means of survival, and policy must account for its reality.
takeaways: The informal economy operates outside state regulation and taxation
It employs the majority of workers globally in many regions
Informal work is the primary economy, not the exception

faq.question: How large is the global informal economy?
faq.answer: The International Labour Organization estimates that over 60% of the world's workforce operates in the informal economy. In sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, the figure exceeds 80%. Informal work is the norm for most humans, not formal wage employment.

faq.question: Should governments formalize the informal economy?
faq.answer: Opinions differ. Formalization can bring protections, taxation revenue, and rights. But it can also destroy flexible arrangements that work for participants and impose bureaucratic costs on the poorest workers. Anthropologists emphasize understanding informal logic before imposing formal structures.
